title: Japan and South Korea Stage Rare Joint Currency Intervention as Yen Surges 3%
excerpt: The coordinated move sent the yen to its strongest level in six months, while the Bank of Japan held rates steady at 1% and the U.S. Treasury called the currency 'very undervalued.'
body:
• Japan and South Korea coordinated a rare joint intervention in currency markets on Wednesday, sending the yen surging 3% against the dollar to 157.8 — a level not seen since January.
  • The Bank of Japan held interest rates steady at 1% on Thursday, disappointing those who expected a rate hike to support the weakening yen.
  • U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the yen was "very undervalued," in a signal that Washington would not oppose Japan's efforts to prop up its currency.
  • The coordinated move came after months of yen weakness, with Tokyo having spent $70 billion defending the currency during April and May alone.

A Rare Alliance in Currency Markets

Japan and South Korea launched a coordinated intervention in foreign exchange markets on Wednesday, marking a rare joint effort by two of Asia's largest economies to defend their currencies against a persistently strong U.S. dollar. The move sent the yen surging approximately 3% to 157.8 against the dollar — its strongest level in six months.

The intervention was widely seen as a tactical escalation after months of yen weakness that had pushed the Japanese currency past 163 per dollar earlier this month, a 38-year low. The won also strengthened sharply, with South Korea's finance ministry confirming it had taken "smoothing operations" in coordination with Japanese authorities.

BOJ Stays Pat on Rates

A day after the intervention, the Bank of Japan opted to hold its benchmark interest rate steady at 1% at its two-day policy meeting that concluded Thursday. The decision was expected by most market participants, though some had speculated the central bank might hike to reinforce the intervention's message.

BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda told reporters the central bank would continue to raise rates "if the economy and prices move in line with our forecasts," but gave no timeline. The central bank left its quarterly growth and inflation projections largely unchanged.

"The yen is very undervalued."

— Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury Secretary

Washington Gives a Green Light

In an unusual public endorsement, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the yen was "very undervalued," a signal that Washington would not oppose Japan's intervention. The remark was notable because U.S. administrations typically refrain from commenting on other nations' currency operations, and Japan has historically been sensitive about drawing American criticism for market manipulation.

The statement effectively gave Tokyo cover to continue intervening if needed. Japan spent approximately $70 billion buying yen in April and May after the currency slid past 160 against the dollar, and the latest operation suggests officials remain prepared to deploy reserves at scale.

Impact on Asian Markets and the Rupee

The yen's sudden strengthening rippled across Asian markets. Japanese exporters, which benefit from a weak yen, saw shares retreat. The Nikkei 225 dropped 1.2% on Thursday morning before recovering to close flat.

For Indian markets, the intervention carries mixed implications. A stronger yen tends to reduce competitive pressure on Indian IT services exports to Japan — India's third-largest IT client — but can also prompt broader dollar weakness that lifts emerging-market currencies, including the rupee. The rupee held steady near 84.5 on Thursday, with traders noting that the Reserve Bank of India has its own substantial reserves to manage volatility.

What to Watch

The durability of the yen's recovery will depend on whether the BOJ signals a rate hike at its September meeting and whether the Federal Reserve begins cutting rates later this year. Traders will also watch Japan's reserves data for clues on the scale of Wednesday's intervention. For global investors, including the large Indian diaspora population in Japan, the intervention underscores the growing fragility of the post-pandemic currency order.
